docs.text: tsne-h2pack ¶ t-SNE in linear time, for millions of points, in 2D or 3D. tsne-h2pack computes the all-pairs repulsion of t-SNE with an H² matrix, so every iteration costs O(N) instead of O(N²). It follows the scikit-learn interface, so most existing code needs only a new import; see the differences . pip install tsne-h2pack from tsne_h2pack import TSNE Y = TSNE ( n_jobs = 8 ) . fit_transform ( X ) Wheels for Linux x86-64 and Apple Silicon macOS, Python 3.10–3.14. 1,306,127 mouse brain cells, 39 cell types. 106 seconds end to end on 12 cores of an Apple M5 Max laptop. O(N) cost per iteration, from an H² matrix of the kernel 69 s for 1M points end to end, 12 threads, k-NN included 2D & 3D same algorithm and code path in either dimension sklearn-style API fit_transform with scikit-learn's parameter names The idea in one picture ¶ The repulsive force needs the product of a dense N × N kernel matrix with the embedding. tsne-h2pack never forms that matrix. Nearby points interact through small dense blocks along the diagonal, computed exactly. Distant groups interact through low-rank blocks, whose bases are nested across the levels of a spatial tree. The nesting makes both building and applying the matrix linear in N, at a chosen accuracy. One product then gives the full repulsive force and its normalization. Read how it works → Time grows roughly linearly with N ¶ Optimization time on 12 threads (Apple M5 Max), 1000 iterations, mouse brain cells in 50 PCA dimensions: Embedding 50K points 100K 250K 500K 1M 2D 2.2 s 3.5 s 7.7 s 15.1 s 27.8 s 3D 7.4 s 17.6 s 39.3 s 106.6 s 172.4 s In 2D, doubling the data roughly doubles the time. Going from 1 to 12 threads speeds the optimization up 3.8–6.2× in 2D and 7.4–10.2× in 3D, depending on size. The advantage shows from about 50K points; below about 10K, any t-SNE library is fast. docs.text: API reference ¶ tsne_h2pack.TSNE ¶ TSNE ( n_components : int = 2 , perplexity : float = 30.0 , early_exaggeration : float = 12.0 , learning_rate : Union [ float , str ] = "auto" , max_iter : int = 1000 , n_iter_without_progress : int = 300 , min_grad_norm : float = 1e-07 , metric : str = "euclidean" , init : Union [ str , ndarray ] = "pca" , verbose : int = 0 , random_state : Optional [ int ] = None , method : str = "h2pack" , n_jobs : Optional [ int ] = None , h2_tol : Optional [ float ] = None , h2_rebuild_freq : Optional [ int ] = None , enable_profiling : bool = False , profiling_output_file : Optional [ str ] = None , knn_method : str = "pynndescent" , knn_params : Optional [ dict ] = None , h2_rebuild_freq_early : Optional [ int ] = None , h2_leaf_size : Optional [ int ] = None , ) t-SNE: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding with H2Pack acceleration. Drop-in replacement for sklearn.manifold.TSNE with identical API. Parameters: n_components ( int , default: 2 ) – Dimension of the embedded space. perplexity ( float , default: 30.0 ) – The perplexity is related to the number of nearest neighbors that is used in other manifold learning algorithms. Larger datasets usually require a larger perplexity. Consider selecting a value between 5 and 50. Different values can result in significantly different results. early_exaggeration ( float , default: 12.0 ) – Controls how tight natural clusters in the original space are in the embedded space and how much space will be between them. learning_rate ( float or auto , default: 'auto' ) – The learning rate. 'auto' uses max(n_samples / 12, 200) , the rule FIt-SNE and openTSNE use: a fixed rate of a few hundred badly under-converges once n_samples reaches the tens of thousands. max_iter ( int , default: 1000 ) – Maximum number of iterations for the optimization. n_iter_without_progress ( int , default: 300 ) – Maximum number of iterations without progress before we abort the optimization. min_grad_norm ( float , default: 1e-7 ) – If the gradient norm is below this threshold, the optimization will be stopped. metric ( ( euclidean , precomputed ) , default: 'euclidean' ) – 'euclidean': X is a feature array and the k-NN graph is built with knn_method . 'precomputed': X is a sparse (n_samples, n_samples) matrix of k-NN distances (not squared), as returned by sklearn.neighbors.kneighbors_graph(..., mode='distance') or any other k-NN library; every row needs more than perplexity neighbors (3 * perplexity is what the 'euclidean' path uses). The k-NN search is skipped, so several runs, or several libraries, can share one graph. init ( ( random , pca ) , default: 'random' ) – Initialization of the embedding. 'pca' follows scikit-learn: the PCA projection of X ( svd_solver='randomized' , seeded with random_state ) rescaled so that the first coordinate has standard deviation 1e-4; it usually preserves the global structure better. 'random' draws each coordinate from N(0, 1e-4) in the C extension. PCA needs features, so with metric='precomputed' an init of 'pca' falls back to 'random' with a warning (pass init='random' to silence it). An ndarray is used as the initial embedding as is (no rescaling). .. versionchanged:: 3.3.0 The default changed from 'random' to 'pca', as in scikit-learn 1.2. verbose ( int , default: 0 ) – Verbosity level. If > 0, prints progress information. random_state ( int or None , default: None ) – Random seed for reproducibility. method ( str , default: 'h2pack' ) – Method for repulsive force computation: - 'h2pack': Use H2Pack for O(N) computation (default) - 'exact': Use direct O(N²) computation n_jobs ( int or None , default: None ) – Number of threads for the k-NN search, the optimizer and H2Pack. None means 1 thread; -1 means all cores (joblib convention). h2_tol ( float , default: None ) – H2Pack low-rank approximation tolerance. Lower values = more accurate but slower. None selects the default for n_components (see H2_DEFAULTS ; 1e-2 in 2D, which already reproduces the embedding quality of an FFT (openTSNE) run). Only used when method='h2pack'. h2_rebuild_freq ( int , default: None ) – The H2 matrix is rebuilt, and the repulsive force recomputed, every this many iterations; in between, the last repulsive force is reused. Lower values = more accurate but slower (in 2D, 2 is slightly better than FIt-SNE's quality, 3 is on par). None selects the default for n_components . Only used when method='h2pack'. h2_rebuild_freq_early ( int , default: None ) – Rebuild frequency during early exaggeration (after the first 20 iterations), a phase that is insensitive to a delayed repulsive force. Never lower than h2_rebuild_freq . None selects the default for n_components . h2_leaf_size ( int , default: None ) – Maximum number of points per H2 leaf box. Affects speed and memory only, not accuracy. None selects the default for n_components . enable_profiling ( bool , default: False ) – Enable detailed profiling of computation time breakdown. profiling_output_file ( str or None , default: None ) – Path to save profiling CSV data. If None, uses default name. knn_method ( str , default: 'pynndescent' ) – k-NN method for finding nearest neighbors: - 'pynndescent': PyNNDescent approximate k-NN (default, ~96% recall, auto-tuning) - 'exact': sklearn brute-force exact k-NN - 'balltree': sklearn ball tree exact k-NN - 'faiss': FAISS approximate k-NN (CPU-only, very fast) - 'annoy': Annoy approximate k-NN (memory-efficient) knn_params ( dict or None , default: None ) – Method-specific parameters for k-NN computation. See _knn_methods.py for details on each method's parameters. Common parameters: PyNNDescent (auto-tuning default): - n_trees: Number of RP trees (None=auto, default varies by dataset size) - n_iters: Search iterations (None=auto, default varies by dataset size) - metric: Distance metric (default='euclidean') FAISS: - index_type: 'Flat', 'IVFFlat', 'IVFPQ', 'HNSW' (default='IVFFlat') - nlist: Number of clusters for IVF (default=100) - nprobe: Clusters to search (default=10) - use_gpu: Use GPU if available (default=False) Annoy: - n_trees: Number of trees (default=50) - search_k: Search depth (default=-1, auto) Attributes: embedding_ ( ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components) ) – Stores the embedding vectors. kl_divergence_ ( float ) – Kullback-Leibler divergence after optimization. n_iter_ ( int ) – Number of iterations run. Examples: >>> from tsne_h2pack import TSNE >>> import numpy as np >>> X = np . random . randn ( 1000 , 50 ) >>> tsne = TSNE ( n_components = 2 , perplexity = 30 , random_state = 42 ) >>> Y = tsne . fit_transform ( X ) >>> print ( Y . shape ) (1000, 2) fit_transform ¶ fit_transform ( X : ndarray , y = None ) -> np . ndarray Fit X into an embedded space and return that transformed output. Parameters: X ( ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features) ) – Input data. y ( Ignored , default: None ) – Not used, present for API consistency by sklearn convention. Returns: X_new ( ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components) ) – Embedding of the training data in low-dimensional space.

docs.text: Benchmarks ¶ All numbers come from the project's benchmark suite, run in November 2026 on an Apple M5 Max (12 performance cores, 6 efficiency cores, 36 GB) under macOS 27.2 with tsne-h2pack 3.2.0. Thread counts are 1, 4, 8 and 12. Times are in seconds. Setup ¶ Data. The 10x Genomics mouse brain cells, 50 PCA components, subsampled to 50K–1M points. Pipeline. PyNNDescent k-NN graph with k = 90, perplexity 30, random initialization, 1000 iterations of which the first 250 use early exaggeration 12, and learning_rate="auto" . Defaults only. One configuration for every size, with no per-size tuning. Quality. KL divergence against a common P, and the fraction of each point's 10 nearest neighbors preserved in the embedding. 2D: scaling with data size and threads ¶ Points Optimization, 1 thread (s) 4 threads (s) 8 threads (s) 12 threads (s) Speedup, 1 → 12 threads End to end, 12 threads (s) Peak memory (GB) 50K 8.2 2.7 2.2 2.2 3.8× 4.1 1.4 100K 18.2 5.4 4.0 3.5 5.2× 7.5 2.2 250K 42.2 14.0 9.4 7.7 5.5× 18.1 4.2 500K 85.8 27.9 18.2 15.1 5.7× 36.3 9.1 1M 171.8 56.8 37.5 27.8 6.2× 69.3 15.7 Times are means of 3 runs (2 runs at 500K, 1 run at 1M). Optimization time grows roughly linearly with N: doubling the data roughly doubles the time. Four threads give a 3.0–3.4× speedup at every size. Beyond that, parallel efficiency improves with size, because larger problems give each thread more work per synchronization; at 50K points the eight-to-twelve-thread step gains nothing. "End to end" includes the k-NN search and the P matrix. At 1M points on 12 threads it splits into 35 s for the k-NN graph, 7 s for P and setup, and 28 s for the optimization. Once the optimizer is this fast, the neighbor search is the largest cost. Inside the optimization ¶ Share of the 2D optimization time on 12 threads: Points Attractive forces H² rebuild H² product Other 50K 20% 37% 31% 13% 250K 22% 39% 30% 8% 1M 28% 38% 30% 3% The H² matrix is rebuilt every third iteration and multiplied once per rebuild. Together these take about two thirds of the time. See How it works for what each part does. 3D: scaling with data size and threads ¶ tsne-h2pack runs unchanged with n_components=3 , using the 3D default h2_tol=3e-2 . Each 3D size was run once. Points Optimization, 1 thread (s) 4 threads (s) 8 threads (s) 12 threads (s) Speedup, 1 → 12 threads End to end, 12 threads (s) Peak memory (GB) 50K 54.8 16.4 9.1 7.4 7.4× 9.3 1.2 100K 178.6 42.1 22.9 17.6 10.2× 21.7 2.3 250K 288.8 86.4 49.5 39.3 7.4× 49.8 5.1 500K 930.0 263.7 146.4 106.6 8.7× 127.4 9.5 1M 1273.1 361.7 219.3 172.4 7.4× 214.5 16.3 3D costs 3–7× as much as 2D at the same N on 12 threads. The kernel's numerical rank is higher in 3D, about 40 at the default tolerance against about 10–17 in 2D. The 3D times are less regular in N than the 2D ones: the attractive-force pass costs about twice as much per point at 100K and 500K as at the neighboring sizes, at every thread count. Thread scaling is better than in 2D because the H² rebuild, the largest part, parallelizes well. FFT-accelerated t-SNE does not support 3D, so other libraries fall back to Barnes-Hut trees there. In the same suite, their optimization took about 5–10× longer than tsne-h2pack's on 4 threads, 8–19× longer on 8 and 9–16× longer on 12, and tsne-h2pack's embeddings had lower KL divergence and better neighbor preservation at every size. Comparison to other t-SNE implementations ¶ To compare gradient methods fairly, openTSNE and FIt-SNE were given the same k-NN graph and the same P as tsne-h2pack, so only the optimization differs. Each library used its own default learning-rate rule. 2D optimization time in seconds, on log scales, for 1, 4, 8 and 12 threads. UMAP is shown for reference; it optimizes a different objective. 2D optimization time on 12 threads: Points tsne-h2pack (s) FIt-SNE (s) openTSNE (s) 50K 2.2 25.1 57.3 250K 7.7 45.3 213.9 1M 27.8 130.8 800.3 The three t-SNE embeddings reach matching quality at every size: KL within 2.5% and neighbor preservation within 0.014 of the best of the three. openTSNE's macOS wheel is built without OpenMP, so its times do not change with the thread count on a Mac. Comparison to UMAP ¶ UMAP optimizes a different objective, so its KL and neighbor-preservation scores are not directly comparable. On its own defaults and a k = 15 graph from the same k-NN code, UMAP's optimization took 3.0 s at 50K and 121 s at 1M points on 12 threads. tsne-h2pack took 2.2 s and 28 s. Caveats ¶ Learning rate. tsne-h2pack keeps scikit-learn's factor 4 in the gradient. Libraries that drop it take a 4× smaller step at the same nominal learning rate, so "auto" rules are not identical across libraries. Self-reported KL. Each library computes its own KL, so those numbers are not comparable. The quality numbers here are all recomputed against one common P. Memory. tsne-h2pack's peak memory is 16 GB at 1M points in both 2D and 3D, somewhat more than FFT-based implementations need. Hardware. One laptop. macOS decides which cores run the threads, and some work may have landed on the slower efficiency cores, so the times are an upper bound on what the hardware can do. Thread scaling on server cores can differ. Reproducing the benchmarks ¶ The suite lives in the benchmarks/ folder of the repository. Its README describes the protocol, and config.py holds the sizes, thread counts and repetitions. The full sweep takes several hours on a laptop.

Each library used its own default learning-rate rule. 2D optimization time in seconds, on log scales, for 1, 4, 8 and 12 threads. UMAP is shown for reference; it optimizes a different objective. 2D optimization time on 12 threads: Points tsne-h2pack (s) FIt-SNE (s) openTSNE (s) 50K 2.2 25.1 57.3 250K 7.7 45.3 213.9 1M 27.8 130.8 800.3 The three t-SNE embeddings reach matching quality at every size: KL within 2.5% and neighbor preservation within 0.014 of the best of the three. openTSNE's macOS wheel is built without OpenMP, so its times do not change with the thread count on a Mac.
docs.title: Comparison to other t-SNE implementations

docs.text: UMAP optimizes a different objective, so its KL and neighbor-preservation scores are not directly comparable. On its own defaults and a k = 15 graph from the same k-NN code, UMAP's optimization took 3.0 s at 50K and 121 s at 1M points on 12 threads. tsne-h2pack took 2.2 s and 28 s.
docs.title: Comparison to UMAP

docs.text: Learning rate. tsne-h2pack keeps scikit-learn's factor 4 in the gradient. Libraries that drop it take a 4× smaller step at the same nominal learning rate, so "auto" rules are not identical across libraries. Self-reported KL. Each library computes its own KL, so those numbers are not comparable. The quality numbers here are all recomputed against one common P. Memory. tsne-h2pack's peak memory is 16 GB at 1M points in both 2D and 3D, somewhat more than FFT-based implementations need. Hardware. One laptop. macOS decides which cores run the threads, and some work may have landed on the slower efficiency cores, so the times are an upper bound on what the hardware can do. Thread scaling on server cores can differ.
docs.title: Caveats

docs.text: The suite lives in the benchmarks/ folder of the repository. Its README describes the protocol, and config.py holds the sizes, thread counts and repetitions. The full sweep takes several hours on a laptop.

docs.text: Changelog ¶ All notable changes to tsne-h2pack will be documented in this file. The format is based on Keep a Changelog , and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning . [Unreleased] ¶ [3.3.1] - 2026-11-09 ¶ Installs and runs on every CPython from 3.10 to 3.14, checked automatically in CI. Added ¶ Wheels for Python 3.14 (Linux x86-64 and macOS arm64). CI runs the test suite on Python 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 on Linux and macOS (was 3.10 and 3.12), installs the pynndescent extra the way users do, and runs the defaults on 20,000 points, large enough to take PyNNDescent's NN-descent path. Every wheel is tested the same way after it is built. Changed ¶ Python 3.10 or newer is required ( requires-python = ">=3.10" ; was 3.8). Python 3.8 and 3.9 are end-of-life (October 2024 and October 2025), and neither was tested before. On 3.9 the newest PyNNDescent (0.7.0) crashes inside numba 0.60, the newest numba for 3.9, which broke the default knn_method='pynndescent' above a few thousand points, and the test suite failed on GitHub's macOS runner. No more wheels are built for 3.9; 3.3.0 stays installable there. Fixed ¶ With the default init='pca' , NumPy 2.0-2.2 on macOS (2.2 is the newest NumPy for Python 3.10) printed about fifty spurious RuntimeWarning: divide by zero / overflow / invalid value encountered in matmul from scikit-learn's randomized PCA, although the result was exact (numpy/numpy#28687). They are silenced around the PCA only; a non-finite PCA result now raises a clear error. The Annoy self-check in the test suite runs in a child process: a broken Annoy build can segfault (GitHub's macOS runner, Python 3.11), which killed the whole pytest run. [3.3.0] - 2026-11-05 ¶ PCA initialization, now the default as in scikit-learn, and the benchmarks rerun on an Apple M5 Max at 1, 4, 8 and 12 threads. Added ¶ init='pca' , as in scikit-learn: the randomized PCA of X (seeded with random_state ), rescaled so the first coordinate has standard deviation 1e-4. Computed in Python (0.5 s at 1M x 50) and handed to C through the new tsne_params_t.init_Y field (appended; the struct is now 160 bytes). init also accepts an ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components), used as is, also with metric='precomputed' . Changed ¶ The default initialization is now init='pca' , as in scikit-learn 1.2+ (was 'random' ). On Zheng 100K / 250K (same P, 3 seeds) PCA init gives clearly better global structure (Spearman correlation of high- vs low-dimensional distances 0.54 / 0.56 vs 0.49 / 0.47, and far less seed-dependent), the same 10-NN preservation and a 0.2-0.5% higher common-P KL, at no cost in optimization time. Pass init='random' for the previous behavior. With metric='precomputed' there are no features to project, so init='pca' (the default) falls back to random initialization with a UserWarning ; scikit-learn raises instead. Pass init='random' to silence it. The benchmark scripts pin init='random' , the protocol every library is compared under. Benchmarks ¶ All suites were rerun on an Apple M5 Max at 1, 4, 8 and 12 threads: 2D and 3D sweeps on the 10x mouse brain cells, the GloVe out-of-the-box comparison and the full 1.3M-cell run (see benchmarks/ ). Headline 2D numbers (optimization on the same P): 2.1-4.0x faster than FIt-SNE on one thread, 2.9-9.7x on four, 3.9-11.4x on eight and 4.7-11.6x on twelve; 1M points in 27.8 s of optimization and 69 s end to end on 12 threads. 3D: 5.3-18.5x faster than FIt-SNE's Barnes-Hut at better quality. Full 1.3M cells end to end: 106 s on 12 threads. benchmarks/config.py runs 1, 4, 8 and 12 threads; report.py prints a thread-scaling table per thread count; new benchmarks/hero_zheng.py for the full-dataset run. Build ¶ The macOS wheels now require macOS 15 ( macosx_15_0_arm64 ; was 14). GitHub retired its macOS 14 runners on 2026-11-02, and the Homebrew OpenBLAS and GCC runtime libraries bundled into the wheel on the macOS 15 runners are built for macOS 15. On macOS 14, pip builds from the source distribution (needs Homebrew gcc and openblas ). CI runs its macOS jobs on macos-15 . On macOS 27 the H2Pack makefile needs MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET set (e.g. 14.0): GCC 12 otherwise derives -mmacosx-version-min=18.0 from the Darwin version and the assembler rejects it. setup.py already sets it for the extension. Repository ¶ Prepared for the public release: maintainer scripts moved to scripts/ , a development guide in docs/DEVELOPMENT.md , superseded pre-September-2026 benchmark results and the old hand-written site removed, project links point to GitHub and the documentation site. [3.2.0] - 2026-10-07 ¶ 3D got a real tuning pass: per-dimension H2 defaults, the tree-order renumbering in any dimension, and proxy points selected at h2_tol . Zheng 1M in 3D at 8 threads: 857 s -> 362 s optimization for the same embedding quality; vs FIt-SNE's Barnes-Hut (its only 3D mode) 9.6-24x faster on identical P ( benchmarks/results_3d/REPORT.md ). 2D results are unchanged apart from ~10% from the proxy-point change. Changed ¶ H2 settings default to None and resolve per embedding dimension ( tsne_h2pack.H2_DEFAULTS , h2_defaults(n_components) ): 2D unchanged ( h2_tol=1e-2 , rebuild 3/10, leaf 100); 3D uses h2_tol=3e-2 (rank 41 instead of 58; 13-20% faster at 8 threads, common-P KL +0.1-0.2%, 10-NN preservation equal or higher on Zheng 250K / 1M). Tuning grid on one shared P: leaf size flat 50-150, rebuild every 2 / 4 / 6 = -0.1% / +0.35% / +2% KL, h2_tol 1e-1 another ~20% faster for +0.5% KL. Explicit values still win. Performance ¶ Points are renumbered along the H2 tree order in any embedding dimension (it was 2D-only). The generic attractive pass gathers Y[d*n + j] per neighbor and became cache-miss bound at scale in 3D (grew like N^1.7): Zheng 1M / 8 threads, 3D, attractive 562 -> 147 s, optimization 856 -> 440 s; embedding unchanged. Proxy points are selected at the run's h2_tol (clamped to [1e-6, 1e-2]) instead of a fixed 1e-4 left over from the old default. Fewer proxy points make every node's ID cheaper on every rebuild; the ID never resolved the kernel below h2_tol anyway, so quality is unchanged. 3D, GloVe 250K, 8 threads: 312 -> 146 proxy points per box, U-build 96 -> 39 s, optimization 163 -> 106 s. 2D: 58 -> 33 points, optimization 17.3 -> 15.4 s. Cache files are now proxy_v2_<dim>d_f<bits>_tol<tol>.txt ( TSNE_PROXY_TOL overrides for experiments). TSNE_H2_TIMERS=1 also prints H2RANK max=... mean=... (H2 rank over all nodes and rebuilds). Benchmarks ¶ 3D, out of the box on GloVe 250K / 8 threads: the H2 rank is ~59 (2D: 17) and the U-build dominates the rebuild; h2_leaf_size does not help in 3D (100 = 200 < 400 < 800), the proxy tolerance does (above). FIt-SNE's FFT path is 1D/2D only and returns garbage for no_dims=3 without an error (negative "cost"); its Barnes-Hut mode takes 1138.8 s end-to-end (KL 4.900, 10-NN 0.213) vs 147.9 s for tsne-h2pack (KL 4.616, 10-NN 0.231): 7.7x end-to-end, 10.3x on the optimization. BENCH_DIM=3 python sweep.py : the whole suite in 3D ( results_3d/ ), FIt-SNE and openTSNE on their Barnes-Hut gradient. Zheng 50K-1M, shared P, 1 and 8 threads: tsne-h2pack optimization 4.5-14x (1 thread) / 9.6-24x (8 threads) faster than FIt-SNE Barnes-Hut, KL 2-4% lower, 10-NN preservation higher at every size; 1M / 8 threads 362 s vs 5475 s. Where the speedup over FIt-SNE comes from (GloVe 250K, one P): at 1 thread the advantage over FIt-SNE is the reuse alone (H2 per evaluation ~15% slower than the FFT step); at 8 threads 1.7x from H2's parallel scaling x 2.4x from reuse. FIt-SNE's FFT stage is serial (Amdahl serial fraction 0.32). In 3D H2 is 3.7-5x faster per evaluation than Barnes-Hut. [3.1.1] - 2026-09-20 ¶ Quality fix for the default k-NN path; anyone who ran 3.1.0 with the default knn_method on more than 10,000 samples should re-run. Fixed ¶ knn_method='pynndescent' (the default above 10,000 samples) listed every point as its own nearest neighbor. NNDescent.neighbor_graph returns the query point in each row (distance 0); the wrapper kept it, so P got a distance-0 self entry per row and one real neighbor fewer than requested. The self entry absorbed a large share of the row's perplexity budget: on GloVe-100 (20K), common-P KL 4.49 -> 3.87 and 10-NN preservation 0.16 -> 0.24 after the fix (FIt-SNE: 3.80 / 0.24). Exact, ball-tree, FAISS and Annoy paths and metric='precomputed' were not affected. The backend now also strips explicit diagonal entries from any k-NN graph it is given. The k-NN CSR is column-sorted before the perplexity search on every path, so the same graph gives the same P whether it comes from a k-NN method (rows ordered by distance) or from metric='precomputed' (rows ordered by index). Performance ¶ verbose=1 no longer costs ~180 s at 1M points: the progress KL was a serial pass over all of P every 10 iterations; it now runs on all threads at the 50-iteration print cadence. Benchmarks ¶ benchmarks/oob_compare.py + oob_visualize.py : out-of-the-box comparison (each library with its own defaults). GloVe-100, 1.18M points: tsne-h2pack 3.02x faster end-to-end at 8 threads (276.9 vs 835.8 s), 1.86x at 1 thread; common-P KL 5.93 vs 6.23 and exact 10-NN preservation 0.151 vs 0.124 in its favor, because FIt-SNE's Annoy defaults reach 48.7% recall on this data vs 89.1% for pynndescent. benchmarks/results/oob_glove/REPORT.md . [3.1.0] - 2026-09-20 ¶ First release on PyPI. The optimization phase is 2.0-3.4x faster than FIt-SNE on one thread and 4.3-8.8x on eight at matched embedding quality (same k-NN graph and P; Zheng 10x, 50K-1M points; benchmarks/results/REPORT.md ). Two correctness fixes below change results relative to 3.0.x, as do the new defaults for learning_rate , h2_tol and h2_rebuild_freq . Fixed ¶ Perplexity calibration collapsed to a uniform P for large-magnitude distances. The sigma search clamped the exponent at -700; when squared k-NN distances were large relative to the starting sigma (e.g. MNIST in 0-255 pixel units) every neighbor hit the clamp, the row looked uniform, and the bisection walked the wrong way, so P came out as exactly 1/k per neighbor (perplexity = k instead of 30). Now bisects on beta with min-shifted distances; P matches openTSNE's to 2e-6. Divergence when the H2 matrix is not rebuilt every iteration. Between rebuilds the stale kernel weights were multiplied by the current Y, so the repulsion of a pair grew linearly with how far it had separated since the build. The repulsive force from the last rebuild is now reused as a whole until the next rebuild (bounded, slightly delayed gradient), which also skips the matvec on those iterations. Packaging ¶ The sdist no longer picks up binaries left in tsne_h2pack/_lib/ by a local build ( MANIFEST.in ); wheels still get the extension and libH2Pack.so from build_ext . release_preflight.sh : version consistency, submodule reachability, full pytest, sdist + wheel build, twine check , delocate, fresh-venv wheel and sdist installs. wheels.yml : manual dispatch can upload the artifacts to TestPyPI as a dry run. Changed ¶ metric='precomputed' : fit_transform accepts a sparse matrix of k-NN distances (as sklearn's TSNE does) and skips the neighbor search, so runs and libraries can share one graph. knn_method='pynndescent' (the default) uses exact brute-force search below 10,000 samples, unless n_trees / n_iters are passed explicitly. NN-descent is at its worst when k = 3 x perplexity is a large share of a small dataset, and the graph was poor enough to show in the embedding (Zheng 5K: common-P KL 1.61 -> 1.44, kNN-preservation 0.40 -> 0.44, now on par with FIt-SNE). Benchmark suite rewritten as one suite under benchmarks/ ( config.py , sweep.py , run.py , methods.py , data.py , quality.py , report.py ; see its README). One configuration per library (no "fast" variants); every library on its own 'auto' learning-rate rule; all three t-SNE libraries optimize the same P from one shared pynndescent k-NN graph (FIt-SNE loads it as precomputed affinities); common-P quality gate; k-NN / setup / optimization breakdown at 1 and 8 threads; minimum size 50K. benchmarks_opentsne/ and the examples/benchmark_threading_* scripts are removed; their old results are not comparable. learning_rate defaults to 'auto' = max(n_samples / 12, 200) (FIt-SNE's rule; note this gradient carries the sklearn factor 4, FIt-SNE's does not). h2_tol default 1e-4 -> 1e-2 ; h2_rebuild_freq default 2 -> 3 . New h2_rebuild_freq_early (default 10): rebuild frequency during early exaggeration. New h2_leaf_size (default 100; H2Pack's 2D default was 200). Performance ¶ Proxy points (data-independent, 7 s to select on one thread) are cached per user in ~/.cache/tsne_h2pack ( TSNE_H2PACK_CACHE_DIR overrides, TSNE_H2PACK_NO_PROXY_CACHE=1 disables); each run works on a private copy. Fixed start-up cost 8.2 s -> 0.2 s on one thread. Fused 3-column H2 matvec ( src/tsne_h2_matmul.c ): W*[1|Y0|Y1] in one traversal, no BLAS calls on the rank-~10 far-field blocks (matvec 2x faster at 1 thread, 3.5x at 8). 2D attractive pass: interleaved Y gather, register accumulation, blocked vectorized divide (2.4x faster at 1 thread). (1+r^2)^-2 evaluated directly rather than through H2Pack's generic pow() kernel. Points are renumbered along the H2 tree order six times during the run so the attractive pass gathers from nearby memory (1.8x faster attractive pass at 500K); undone on output. The attractive pass divides in float32 (differences still formed in double): ~15% faster, embedding quality unchanged. H2Pack (submodule): pooled large B/D blocks across rebuilds (peak RSS 21.6 -> 10.2 GB at 500K, which also makes 1M points fit in 32 GB), dynamically scheduled B/D build, inlined BLAS-1 in the ID's pivoted QR. H2 rebuild, second round (all results bit-identical unless noted; 500K points, 8 threads): H2Pack tree partition built with OpenMP tasks + chunked stable bucket sort, post-order numbering in a serial post-pass: same tree for any thread count (8.9 -> 2.4 s). H2Pack ID: no one-thread OpenMP team per Householder step, lock-free free_aligned for unpooled blocks (U build 12.1 -> 9.0 s); parallel frees in H2P_destroy (1.3 -> 0.6 s). B/D blocks are no longer stored: each H2 matrix is multiplied once, so the fused matvec evaluates them on the fly into a cache-resident buffer ( TSNE_H2_JIT=0 restores AOT). Rebuild + matvec -2.0 s, peak RSS 10.3 -> 5.9 GB. Root enclosing box and NaN/Inf check fused into one pass (1.26 -> 0.24 s); proxy point sets cached across rebuilds instead of re-read from / re-written to the text file on every rebuild (also fixes a leak of one proxy point set per rebuild). Point renumbering: parallel CSR transposes (six renumberings 4.3 -> 1.6 s). Per-iteration element-wise passes run on all threads; mean of Y and Z are summed block-wise in parallel with thread-count-independent rounding (rounding differs from the old serial sums: embeddings agree to 3e-15 after 5 iterations, quality unchanged). Attractive pass, third round (it had become the largest phase: 41% of the optimization at 500K / 8 threads, half of it at 1 thread). Kernel now in src/tsne_attr_2d.h : float32 copy of P's values (the divide already ran in float32): 12 -> 8 bytes streamed per nonzero, no per-nonzero conversion; refreshed after each renumbering. +4 bytes/nnz of memory until DTYPE is float, when P->values is used directly. neighbors gathered from a float32 copy of Y ( TSNE_ATTR_F32=2 , new default; 1 = previous arithmetic, 0 = all double). Equivalent to the exact force of the embedding rounded to float32 (displacement <= 3.8e-6 per coordinate for |y| < 128, the same in every pair); measured force error 2.5e-5 relative, quality unchanged. Falls back to the double gather for max|y| >= 4096. one (x, y) copy per neighbor, de-interleaved inside the vector loop; blocks of 16. loops written with pointers / size_t counters: setuptools adds CPython's -fno-strict-overflow , which made the int -indexed gather loop 30% slower in the extension than in a standalone build of the same source. dynamic chunk n/(64*threads) in [64, 1024]. Zheng et al. mouse-brain data, optimization only (k-NN excluded), Apple M1 Pro, 1000 iterations, same learning-rate rule, quality measured with a common P: N threads tsne-h2pack FIt-SNE speedup KL (h2pack / FIt-SNE) kNN-pres@10 (h2pack / FIt-SNE) 250K 8 26 s 81 s 3.1x 3.92 / 3.93 0.205 / 0.203 500K 8 53 s 137 s 2.6x 4.48 / 4.50 0.158 / 0.155 1M 8 113 s 354 s 3.1x 5.03 / 5.04 0.116 / 0.114 250K 1 99 s 146 s 1.5x 3.92 / 3.93 0.204 / 0.203 500K 1 200 s 306 s 1.5x 4.48 / 4.50 0.157 / 0.155 1M 1 414 s 715 s 1.7x 5.03 / 5.04 0.117 / 0.114 After the second round (same harness and machine; the table above is the state before it; 500K / 1M at 1 thread not re-run): N threads opt before -> after rebuild + matvec before -> after peak RSS KL / kNN-pres@10 after 250K 8 26.3 -> 22.4 s 14.7 + 3.4 -> 8.3 + 4.9 s 4.9 -> 3.4 GB 3.92 / 0.203 500K 8 53.1 -> 39.5 s 28.3 + 6.4 -> 13.7 + 8.4 s 10.1 -> 5.9 GB 4.48 / 0.157 1M 8 113.4 -> 82.4 s 54.7 + 12.4 -> 23.6 + 16.0 s 18.3 -> 10.9 GB 5.03 / 0.116 250K 1 98.9 -> 94.1 s 46.5 + 12.7 -> 33.8 + 20.4 s 4.9 -> 3.4 GB 3.92 / 0.205 (With JIT blocks the B/D evaluation moves from "rebuild" into "matvec". Wall time improves by a further ~3 s at 500K: the renumbering is not covered by the per-phase timers.) After the third round (attractive pass; same harness and machine): N threads opt before -> after attractive before -> after peak RSS KL / kNN-pres@10 after 250K 8 22.4 -> 15.7 s ~7 -> 3.6 s 3.4 -> 3.6 GB 3.92 / 0.204 500K 8 38.5 -> 29.9 s 16.2 -> 7.7 s 5.9 -> 6.2 GB 4.48 / 0.159 1M 8 82.4 -> 58.7 s ~41 -> 17.9 s 10.9 -> 11.4 GB 5.03 / 0.117 250K 1 94.1 -> 73.7 s ~38 -> 18.8 s 3.4 -> 3.6 GB 3.92 / 0.203 500K 1 -> 144.3 s 86 -> 41.4 s 6.0 GB 4.48 / 0.158 (Before this round: 136 s for 250K on 8 threads, at a fixed learning rate of 200 that left the embedding far less converged -- KL 4.58, kNN-preservation 0.10. openTSNE's FFT takes 282 s at 250K: its macOS wheel is built without OpenMP.) docs.text: Installs and runs on every CPython from 3.10 to 3.14, checked automatically in CI.

Wheels for Python 3.14 (Linux x86-64 and macOS arm64). CI runs the test suite on Python 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 on Linux and macOS (was 3.10 and 3.12), installs the pynndescent extra the way users do, and runs the defaults on 20,000 points, large enough to take PyNNDescent's NN-descent path. docs.text: The default initialization is now init='pca' , as in scikit-learn 1.2+ (was 'random' ). On Zheng 100K / 250K (same P, 3 seeds) PCA init gives clearly better global structure (Spearman correlation of high- vs low-dimensional distances 0.54 / 0.56 vs 0.49 / 0.47, and far less seed-dependent), the same 10-NN preservation and a 0.2-0.5% higher common-P KL, at no cost in optimization time. Pass init='random' for the previous behavior. With metric='precomputed' there are no features to project, so init='pca' (the default) falls back to random initialization with a UserWarning ; scikit-learn raises instead. Pass init='random' to silence it. The benchmark scripts pin init='random' , the protocol every library is compared under.

docs.text: 3D got a real tuning pass: per-dimension H2 defaults, the tree-order renumbering in any dimension, and proxy points selected at h2_tol . Zheng 1M in 3D at 8 threads: 857 s -> 362 s optimization for the same embedding quality; vs FIt-SNE's Barnes-Hut (its only 3D mode) 9.6-24x faster on identical P ( benchmarks/results_3d/REPORT.md ). 2D results are unchanged apart from ~10% from the proxy-point change.

H2 settings default to None and resolve per embedding dimension ( tsne_h2pack.H2_DEFAULTS , h2_defaults(n_components) ): 2D unchanged ( h2_tol=1e-2 , rebuild 3/10, leaf 100); 3D uses h2_tol=3e-2 (rank 41 instead of 58; 13-20% faster at 8 threads, common-P KL +0.1-0.2%, 10-NN preservation equal or higher on Zheng 250K / 1M). Tuning grid on one shared P: leaf size flat 50-150, rebuild every 2 / 4 / 6 = -0.1% / +0.35% / +2% KL, h2_tol 1e-1 another ~20% faster for +0.5% KL. Explicit values still win.

docs.text: Points are renumbered along the H2 tree order in any embedding dimension (it was 2D-only). The generic attractive pass gathers Y[d*n + j] per neighbor and became cache-miss bound at scale in 3D (grew like N^1.7): Zheng 1M / 8 threads, 3D, attractive 562 -> 147 s, optimization 856 -> 440 s; embedding unchanged. Proxy points are selected at the run's h2_tol (clamped to [1e-6, 1e-2]) instead of a fixed 1e-4 left over from the old default. Fewer proxy points make every node's ID cheaper on every rebuild; the ID never resolved the kernel below h2_tol anyway, so quality is unchanged. 3D, GloVe 250K, 8 threads: 312 -> 146 proxy points per box, U-build 96 -> 39 s, optimization 163 -> 106 s. 2D: 58 -> 33 points, optimization 17.3 -> 15.4 s. Cache files are now proxy_v2_<dim>d_f<bits>_tol<tol>.txt ( TSNE_PROXY_TOL overrides for experiments). TSNE_H2_TIMERS=1 also prints H2RANK max=... mean=... (H2 rank over all nodes and rebuilds).
docs.title: Performance

docs.text: 3D, out of the box on GloVe 250K / 8 threads: the H2 rank is ~59 (2D: 17) and the U-build dominates the rebuild; h2_leaf_size does not help in 3D (100 = 200 < 400 < 800), the proxy tolerance does (above). FIt-SNE's FFT path is 1D/2D only and returns garbage for no_dims=3 without an error (negative "cost"); its Barnes-Hut mode takes 1138.8 s end-to-end (KL 4.900, 10-NN 0.213) vs 147.9 s for tsne-h2pack (KL 4.616, 10-NN 0.231): 7.7x end-to-end, 10.3x on the optimization. BENCH_DIM=3 python sweep.py : the whole suite in 3D ( results_3d/ ), FIt-SNE and openTSNE on their Barnes-Hut gradient. Zheng 50K-1M, shared P, 1 and 8 threads: tsne-h2pack optimization 4.5-14x (1 thread) / 9.6-24x (8 threads) faster than FIt-SNE Barnes-Hut, KL 2-4% lower, 10-NN preservation higher at every size; 1M / 8 threads 362 s vs 5475 s. Where the speedup over FIt-SNE comes from (GloVe 250K, one P): at 1 thread the advantage over FIt-SNE is the reuse alone (H2 per evaluation ~15% slower than the FFT step); at 8 threads 1.7x from H2's parallel scaling x 2.4x from reuse. FIt-SNE's FFT stage is serial (Amdahl serial fraction 0.32). In 3D H2 is 3.7-5x faster per evaluation than Barnes-Hut.

docs.text: Quality fix for the default k-NN path; anyone who ran 3.1.0 with the default knn_method on more than 10,000 samples should re-run.

knn_method='pynndescent' (the default above 10,000 samples) listed every point as its own nearest neighbor. NNDescent.neighbor_graph returns the query point in each row (distance 0); the wrapper kept it, so P got a distance-0 self entry per row and one real neighbor fewer than requested. The self entry absorbed a large share of the row's perplexity budget: on GloVe-100 (20K), common-P KL 4.49 -> 3.87 and 10-NN preservation 0.16 -> 0.24 after the fix (FIt-SNE: 3.80 / 0.24). Exact, ball-tree, FAISS and Annoy paths and metric='precomputed' were not affected. The backend now also strips explicit diagonal entries from any k-NN graph it is given. The k-NN CSR is column-sorted before the perplexity search on every path, so the same graph gives the same P whether it comes from a k-NN method (rows ordered by distance) or from metric='precomputed' (rows ordered by index).

docs.text: First release on PyPI. The optimization phase is 2.0-3.4x faster than FIt-SNE on one thread and 4.3-8.8x on eight at matched embedding quality (same k-NN graph and P; Zheng 10x, 50K-1M points; benchmarks/results/REPORT.md ). Two correctness fixes below change results relative to 3.0.x, as do the new defaults for learning_rate , h2_tol and h2_rebuild_freq .

Perplexity calibration collapsed to a uniform P for large-magnitude distances. The sigma search clamped the exponent at -700; when squared k-NN distances were large relative to the starting sigma (e.g. MNIST in 0-255 pixel units) every neighbor hit the clamp, the row looked uniform, and the bisection walked the wrong way, so P came out as exactly 1/k per neighbor (perplexity = k instead of 30). Now bisects on beta with min-shifted distances; P matches openTSNE's to 2e-6. Divergence when the H2 matrix is not rebuilt every iteration. Between rebuilds the stale kernel weights were multiplied by the current Y, so the repulsion of a pair grew linearly with how far it had separated since the build. The repulsive force from the last rebuild is now reused as a whole until the next rebuild (bounded, slightly delayed gradient), which also skips the matvec on those iterations.

docs.text: metric='precomputed' : fit_transform accepts a sparse matrix of k-NN distances (as sklearn's TSNE does) and skips the neighbor search, so runs and libraries can share one graph. knn_method='pynndescent' (the default) uses exact brute-force search below 10,000 samples, unless n_trees / n_iters are passed explicitly. NN-descent is at its worst when k = 3 x perplexity is a large share of a small dataset, and the graph was poor enough to show in the embedding (Zheng 5K: common-P KL 1.61 -> 1.44, kNN-preservation 0.40 -> 0.44, now on par with FIt-SNE). Benchmark suite rewritten as one suite under benchmarks/ ( config.py , sweep.py , run.py , methods.py , data.py , quality.py , report.py ; see its README). One configuration per library (no "fast" variants); every library on its own 'auto' learning-rate rule; all three t-SNE libraries optimize the same P from one shared pynndescent k-NN graph (FIt-SNE loads it as precomputed affinities); common-P quality gate; k-NN / setup / optimization breakdown at 1 and 8 threads; minimum size 50K. benchmarks_opentsne/ and the examples/benchmark_threading_* scripts are removed; their old results are not comparable. learning_rate defaults to 'auto' = max(n_samples / 12, 200) (FIt-SNE's rule; note this gradient carries the sklearn factor 4, FIt-SNE's does not). h2_tol default 1e-4 -> 1e-2 ; h2_rebuild_freq default 2 -> 3 . New h2_rebuild_freq_early (default 10): rebuild frequency during early exaggeration. New h2_leaf_size (default 100; H2Pack's 2D default was 200).

docs.text: Proxy points (data-independent, 7 s to select on one thread) are cached per user in ~/.cache/tsne_h2pack ( TSNE_H2PACK_CACHE_DIR overrides, TSNE_H2PACK_NO_PROXY_CACHE=1 disables); each run works on a private copy. Fixed start-up cost 8.2 s -> 0.2 s on one thread. Fused 3-column H2 matvec ( src/tsne_h2_matmul.c ): W*[1|Y0|Y1] in one traversal, no BLAS calls on the rank-~10 far-field blocks (matvec 2x faster at 1 thread, 3.5x at 8). 2D attractive pass: interleaved Y gather, register accumulation, blocked vectorized divide (2.4x faster at 1 thread). (1+r^2)^-2 evaluated directly rather than through H2Pack's generic pow() kernel. Points are renumbered along the H2 tree order six times during the run so the attractive pass gathers from nearby memory (1.8x faster attractive pass at 500K); undone on output. The attractive pass divides in float32 (differences still formed in double): ~15% faster, embedding quality unchanged. H2Pack (submodule): pooled large B/D blocks across rebuilds (peak RSS 21.6 -> 10.2 GB at 500K, which also makes 1M points fit in 32 GB), dynamically scheduled B/D build, inlined BLAS-1 in the ID's pivoted QR. H2 rebuild, second round (all results bit-identical unless noted; 500K points, 8 threads): H2Pack tree partition built with OpenMP tasks + chunked stable bucket sort, post-order numbering in a serial post-pass: same tree for any thread count (8.9 -> 2.4 s). H2Pack ID: no one-thread OpenMP team per Householder step, lock-free free_aligned for unpooled blocks (U build 12.1 -> 9.0 s); parallel frees in H2P_destroy (1.3 -> 0.6 s). B/D blocks are no longer stored: each H2 matrix is multiplied once, so the fused matvec evaluates them on the fly into a cache-resident buffer ( TSNE_H2_JIT=0 restores AOT). Rebuild + matvec -2.0 s, peak RSS 10.3 -> 5.9 GB. Root enclosing box and NaN/Inf check fused into one pass (1.26 -> 0.24 s); proxy point sets cached across rebuilds instead of re-read from / re-written to the text file on every rebuild (also fixes a leak of one proxy point set per rebuild). Point renumbering: parallel CSR transposes (six renumberings 4.3 -> 1.6 s). Per-iteration element-wise passes run on all threads; mean of Y and Z are summed block-wise in parallel with thread-count-independent rounding (rounding differs from the old serial sums: embeddings agree to 3e-15 after 5 iterations, quality unchanged). Attractive pass, third round (it had become the largest phase: 41% of the optimization at 500K / 8 threads, half of it at 1 thread). Kernel now in src/tsne_attr_2d.h : float32 copy of P's values (the divide already ran in float32): 12 -> 8 bytes streamed per nonzero, no per-nonzero conversion; refreshed after each renumbering. +4 bytes/nnz of memory until DTYPE is float, when P->values is used directly. neighbors gathered from a float32 copy of Y ( TSNE_ATTR_F32=2 , new default; 1 = previous arithmetic, 0 = all double). Equivalent to the exact force of the embedding rounded to float32 (displacement <= 3.8e-6 per coordinate for |y| < 128, the same in every pair); measured force error 2.5e-5 relative, quality unchanged. Falls back to the double gather for max|y| >= 4096. one (x, y) copy per neighbor, de-interleaved inside the vector loop; blocks of 16. loops written with pointers / size_t counters: setuptools adds CPython's -fno-strict-overflow , which made the int -indexed gather loop 30% slower in the extension than in a standalone build of the same source. dynamic chunk n/(64*threads) in [64, 1024]. Zheng et al. mouse-brain data, optimization only (k-NN excluded), Apple M1 Pro, 1000 iterations, same learning-rate rule, quality measured with a common P: N threads tsne-h2pack FIt-SNE speedup KL (h2pack / FIt-SNE) kNN-pres@10 (h2pack / FIt-SNE) 250K 8 26 s 81 s 3.1x 3.92 / 3.93 0.205 / 0.203 500K 8 53 s 137 s 2.6x 4.48 / 4.50 0.158 / 0.155 1M 8 113 s 354 s 3.1x 5.03 / 5.04 0.116 / 0.114 250K 1 99 s 146 s 1.5x 3.92 / 3.93 0.204 / 0.203 500K 1 200 s 306 s 1.5x 4.48 / 4.50 0.157 / 0.155 1M 1 414 s 715 s 1.7x 5.03 / 5.04 0.117 / 0.114 After the second round (same harness and machine; the table above is the state before it; 500K / 1M at 1 thread not re-run): N threads opt before -> after rebuild + matvec before -> after peak RSS KL / kNN-pres@10 after 250K 8 26.3 -> 22.4 s 14.7 + 3.4 -> 8.3 + 4.9 s 4.9 -> 3.4 GB 3.92 / 0.203 500K 8 53.1 -> 39.5 s 28.3 + 6.4 -> 13.7 + 8.4 s 10.1 -> 5.9 GB 4.48 / 0.157 1M 8 113.4 -> 82.4 s 54.7 + 12.4 -> 23.6 + 16.0 s 18.3 -> 10.9 GB 5.03 / 0.116 250K 1 98.9 -> 94.1 s 46.5 + 12.7 -> 33.8 + 20.4 s 4.9 -> 3.4 GB 3.92 / 0.205 (With JIT blocks the B/D evaluation moves from "rebuild" into "matvec". Wall time improves by a further ~3 s at 500K: the renumbering is not covered by the per-phase timers.) After the third round (attractive pass; same harness and machine): N threads opt before -> after attractive before -> after peak RSS KL / kNN-pres@10 after 250K 8 22.4 -> 15.7 s ~7 -> 3.6 s 3.4 -> 3.6 GB 3.92 / 0.204 500K 8 38.5 -> 29.9 s 16.2 -> 7.7 s 5.9 -> 6.2 GB 4.48 / 0.159 1M 8 82.4 -> 58.7 s ~41 -> 17.9 s 10.9 -> 11.4 GB 5.03 / 0.117 250K 1 94.1 -> 73.7 s ~38 -> 18.8 s 3.4 -> 3.6 GB 3.92 / 0.203 500K 1 -> 144.3 s 86 -> 41.4 s 6.0 GB 4.48 / 0.158 (Before this round: 136 s for 250K on 8 threads, at a fixed learning rate of 200 that left the embedding far less converged -- KL 4.58, kNN-preservation 0.10. openTSNE's FFT takes 282 s at 250K: its macOS wheel is built without OpenMP.)

docs.text: Quick start ¶ tsne_h2pack.TSNE follows the scikit-learn interface: create an estimator, then call fit_transform . from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs from tsne_h2pack import TSNE # 20,000 points in 50 dimensions, drawn from 10 clusters X , labels = make_blobs ( n_samples = 20_000 , n_features = 50 , centers = 10 , random_state = 0 ) tsne = TSNE ( n_components = 2 , perplexity = 30 , n_jobs = 8 , random_state = 42 , verbose = 1 ) Y = tsne . fit_transform ( X ) # (20000, 2) print ( tsne . kl_divergence_ , tsne . n_iter_ ) verbose=1 prints progress and the KL divergence every 50 iterations. n_jobs defaults to one thread, so set it to your core count. Differences from scikit-learn ¶ Use fit_transform . fit alone is not implemented, and there is no transform for new points. init defaults to "pca" , as in scikit-learn: the PCA of X , rescaled so the first coordinate has standard deviation 1e-4. "random" and an (n_samples, n_components) array are also accepted. With metric="precomputed" there is no X to project, so "pca" falls back to random initialization with a warning, where scikit-learn raises an error. learning_rate="auto" means max(N / 12, 200) , a larger step than scikit-learn's own "auto" . metric accepts "euclidean" , or "precomputed" with a sparse k-NN distance matrix. A real dataset ¶ This example downloads MNIST from OpenML the first time it runs, which can take a minute or two. from sklearn.datasets import fetch_openml from sklearn.decomposition import PCA import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from tsne_h2pack import TSNE mnist = fetch_openml ( "mnist_784" , version = 1 , as_frame = False ) X = PCA ( n_components = 50 ) . fit_transform ( mnist . data / 255.0 ) labels = mnist . target . astype ( int ) Y = TSNE ( n_jobs = 8 , random_state = 0 , verbose = 1 ) . fit_transform ( X ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 7 )) plt . scatter ( Y [:, 0 ], Y [:, 1 ], c = labels , s = 0.3 , cmap = "tab10" ) plt . axis ( "off" ) plt . show () Reduce to about 50 dimensions first Like other t-SNE implementations, tsne-h2pack works best on PCA-reduced input. It speeds up the k-NN search and removes noise without changing the embedding much. What to read next ¶ How to use tsne-h2pack covers threads, large datasets, perplexity, k-NN backends, precomputed graphs, 3D, and parameters. How it works explains how the H² matrix makes each iteration linear in N. Benchmarks shows timing and quality from 50K to 1M points.

docs.text: How to use tsne-h2pack ¶ Threads ¶ n_jobs defaults to one thread , as in scikit-learn. Set it to your number of physical cores, or n_jobs=-1 for all cores. It controls the k-NN search, the optimizer, and H2Pack's OpenMP threads together. Large datasets ¶ tsne-h2pack's advantage grows with N and is largest from about 50K points up. Below about 10K points any t-SNE library is fast, and scikit-learn works fine. from tsne_h2pack import TSNE tsne = TSNE ( n_components = 2 , perplexity = 30 , learning_rate = "auto" , # max(N / 12, 200) knn_method = "pynndescent" , # default n_jobs = 8 , verbose = 1 , # progress and KL every 50 iterations ) Y = tsne . fit_transform ( X ) # X: (n_samples, n_features), ideally PCA-reduced At 1M points about half of the end-to-end time is the k-NN search, not the optimization. If you embed the same data several times, compute the graph once and reuse it (see Precomputed k-NN graphs ). Memory. Peak memory grows linearly with N, to about 16 GB at 1M points in both 2D and 3D. Perplexity ¶ Perplexity sets roughly how many neighbors each point pays attention to. The default of 30 works for most data; values between 5 and 50 are common, and larger datasets often benefit from larger values. The k-NN search uses 3 × perplexity neighbors, so higher perplexity also costs more time and memory. Choosing a k-NN method ¶ knn_method Kind Notes "pynndescent" approximate, about 90–96% recall Default. Uses exact search below 10K samples. "exact" scikit-learn brute force Exact, slow for large N. Useful to rule out graph error. "balltree" scikit-learn ball tree Exact. Works best in low input dimension. "faiss" FAISS Approximate. Needs faiss-cpu . "annoy" Annoy Approximate, low memory. Needs annoy . Keyword arguments for the backend go in knn_params . For example, knn_params={"n_trees": 30, "n_iters": 10} makes PyNNDescent more accurate and slower. Annoy accepts n_trees and search_k , and FAISS accepts nlist and nprobe . The graph matters more than the optimizer A low-recall k-NN graph degrades the embedding more than any of the gradient approximations do. On GloVe word vectors (1.18M points), PyNNDescent's defaults recover 89% of the true 90 nearest neighbors, while a fast Annoy configuration recovers 49%, with visibly worse neighbor preservation in the embedding. Precomputed k-NN graphs ¶ Pass a SciPy sparse matrix of k-NN distances with metric="precomputed" , as in scikit-learn. The neighbor search is skipped, so several runs, or several libraries, can share one graph. from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors from tsne_h2pack import TSNE k = 90 # 3 x perplexity knn = NearestNeighbors ( n_neighbors = k ) . fit ( X ) . kneighbors_graph ( mode = "distance" ) Y = TSNE ( metric = "precomputed" , perplexity = 30 , n_jobs = 8 , init = "random" ) . fit_transform ( knn ) Each row needs more than perplexity neighbors. Three times the perplexity is the usual choice. Do not include the point itself as a neighbor. A graph has no features for the default PCA initialization. Pass init="random" , as above, or your own starting embedding, for example init=PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X) / 1e4 . Otherwise tsne-h2pack falls back to random initialization and warns. 3D embeddings ¶ Set n_components=3 . The same algorithm runs, because the H² matrix works in both 2D and 3D. Y3 = TSNE ( n_components = 3 , n_jobs = 8 ) . fit_transform ( X ) Expect roughly 3–8× the 2D optimization time at the same N, depending on the size and the thread count. The kernel's numerical rank is higher in 3D: about 40 at the 3D default tolerance, against about 10–17 in 2D. FFT-accelerated t-SNE is limited to 1D and 2D, so in 3D other libraries use Barnes-Hut trees. H² parameters ¶ Most users should not change these. In 2D the defaults reach the same embedding quality as FFT-accelerated t-SNE on the same P. Parameter Default Effect h2_tol 1e-2 in 2D, 3e-2 in 3D Relative accuracy of the H² approximation. Tighter costs time without measurable quality gain. h2_rebuild_freq 3 Rebuild the H² matrix every this many iterations after early exaggeration, reusing the repulsive force in between. 2 is slightly more accurate; 6 and above is visibly worse. h2_rebuild_freq_early 10 Rebuild frequency during early exaggeration, which is insensitive to it. h2_leaf_size 100 Points per leaf box. Speed and memory only. Leaving a parameter at None selects the default for the embedding dimension. Why rebuilding every few iterations is safe, and why the force is reused rather than recomputed, is explained in How it works . Exact repulsion ¶ method="exact" computes the repulsive force directly, without the H² matrix. It costs O(N²) per iteration, so use it only for small data or to check results. Datasets below 2,000 points use the direct computation automatically. Learning rate ¶ learning_rate="auto" is max(N / 12, 200) . A fixed 200, the old scikit-learn default, under-converges badly beyond about 100K points. scikit-learn's own "auto" uses a smaller step, max(N / 48, 50) . Comparing with other libraries tsne-h2pack follows scikit-learn and keeps the factor 4 in the gradient. Libraries that drop it take a 4× smaller step at the same nominal learning rate. Reproducibility ¶ With a fixed random_state , single-threaded runs are bit-for-bit reproducible. Multi-threaded runs are not: the result is statistically equivalent but differs between runs. See Accuracy and reproducibility . Profiling ¶ enable_profiling=True records a per-iteration breakdown into attractive forces, H² rebuild, and H² product. profiling_output_file writes it to CSV.

docs.text: Accuracy and reproducibility ¶ Why a loose tolerance is enough ¶ The default h2_tol asks for about 1% relative accuracy in the kernel approximation in 2D, and 3% in 3D. That sounds loose, but the gradient is already noisy for other reasons: P is built from an approximate k-NN graph with about 90–96% recall. Force reuse delays the repulsive force by up to two iterations. FFT-accelerated t-SNE also approximates the kernel, by interpolation on a grid. Tighter tolerances cost time and give no measurable improvement in KL or neighbor preservation. In 2D, at 1e-2, tsne-h2pack's embeddings match those of FFT-accelerated t-SNE on the same P, from 50K to 1M points. In 3D, 3e-2 changes KL by only 0.1–0.2% compared with 1e-2, and the embeddings score better than Barnes-Hut t-SNE on the same P, in both KL and neighbor preservation. How quality is measured ¶ Self-reported KL values cannot be compared across libraries: each one builds its own P and evaluates the objective in its own way. The benchmarks therefore score every embedding against one common P : KL divergence \(\sum_{ij} p_{ij} \log (p_{ij} / q_{ij})\) with the common P and the exact Q of the embedding. k-NN preservation , the fraction of each point's 10 nearest neighbors in the input that are also among its 10 nearest in the embedding. Two t-SNE embeddings count as matched when each is within 3% in KL and 0.015 in neighbor preservation of the best one. Reproducibility ¶ Setting Bit-reproducible with fixed random_state ? n_jobs=1 Yes n_jobs > 1 No Reductions such as Z are summed in fixed blocks of 4096 points and combined in order, so their rounding does not depend on the thread count. Some parallel steps are still order-dependent, so multi-threaded runs differ between runs in the last bits. t-SNE amplifies tiny differences over 1000 iterations, so the final embeddings differ visibly while their quality stays the same. Use n_jobs=1 when exact reproduction matters.

How it works ¶ The t-SNE gradient ¶ For an embedding \(y_1, \dots, y_N\) , t-SNE uses the Cauchy kernel \[ w_{ij} =  rac{1}{1 + \lVert y_i - y_j Vert^2}, \qquad q_{ij} =  rac{w_{ij}}{Z}, \qquad Z = \sum_{k 
eq l} w_{kl}. \] The gradient of the KL divergence splits into an attractive and a repulsive part: \[  rac{\partial C}{\partial y_i} = 4 \Big( \underbrace{\sum_j p_{ij}\, w_{ij}\, (y_i - y_j)}_{	ext{attractive}} \;-\; \underbrace{ rac{1}{Z} \sum_{j 
eq i} w_{ij}^2\, (y_i - y_j)}_{	ext{repulsive}} \Big). \] The attractive part only involves pairs where \(p_{ij} 
eq 0\) . P comes from a k-NN graph with k = 3 × perplexity, so this is a sparse pass costing O(kN). The repulsive part couples every pair of points. Computed directly it is O(N²) per iteration, which is the reason fast t-SNE methods exist. One kernel gives both force and normalization ¶ Let \(K\) be the \(N 	imes N\) matrix with \(K_{ij} = (1 + \lVert y_i - y_j Vert^2)^{-2} = w_{ij}^2\) off the diagonal and zero on it. The repulsive force is a matrix product: \[ F^{	ext{rep}}_i =  rac{1}{Z}\Big( y_i\, s_i - v_i \Big), \qquad s = K\mathbf{1}, \quad v = K Y. \] The normalization \(Z\) needs \(w_{ij}\) , not \(w_{ij}^2\) . Writing \(w_{ij} = (1 + r_{ij}^2)\, K_{ij}\) and expanding \(r_{ij}^2 = \lVert y_iVert^2 + \lVert y_jVert^2 - 2\, y_i \cdot y_j\) gives \[ Z = \sum_i s_i \;+\; 2 \sum_i \lVert y_i Vert^2 s_i \;-\; 2 \sum_i y_i \cdot v_i . \] So a single product \(K \,[\,\mathbf{1} \mid Y\,]\) , with \(d+1\) right-hand sides in \(d\) dimensions, yields the full repulsive force and \(Z\) . H² matrices ¶ \(K\) is dense but smooth away from the diagonal. An H² matrix , built here with H2Pack , 1 exploits that: Partition. The points are split recursively into a tree of boxes, down to leaves of about 100 points. Near field. Blocks between neighboring boxes are evaluated exactly. Far field. A block between two well-separated boxes is low-rank: \(K_{IJ} \approx U_I\, B_{IJ}\, U_J^{	op}\) . Nesting. Each parent's basis \(U\) is expressed through its children's bases, so the bases are never stored in full. Nesting is what separates H² matrices from the simpler H-matrices and from Barnes-Hut trees. For a fixed accuracy, both the construction and the matrix-vector product cost O(N) , not O(N log N). Reusing the repulsive force ¶ The embedding moves slowly, so the H² matrix does not need rebuilding every iteration. tsne-h2pack rebuilds it every iteration for the first 20 iterations, every 10th for the rest of early exaggeration, and every 3rd afterwards. The subtle part is what to do between rebuilds. The tempting approach diverges Keeping the old H² matrix and multiplying it by the current positions looks harmless. It is not. The matrix holds kernel weights for the old positions, so the repulsion between two points grows linearly with how far they have separated since the rebuild, instead of decaying. Outliers get flung outward and the embedding blows up. On 250K mouse brain cells, the embedding grew to a width of 1243 units instead of 235. tsne-h2pack instead reuses the whole repulsive force and Z from the last rebuild until the next one. The force is slightly delayed but bounded, and the product is skipped entirely on those iterations.
